issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar does not exclude a civil court from examining whether a demolition action falls outside the statute or is affected by a jurisdictional error.
material_facts: The statute provided an appeal from a demolition order to an appellate tribunal and a further appeal to an administrator, and purported to bar civil suits concerning demolition proceedings.
The statutory scheme regulated the pre-existing common-law right to construct buildings rather than creating the right or liability itself.
The dispute concerned whether civil courts could examine demolition actions despite the statutory bar.
issues.conclusion: A court should ordinarily direct a person aggrieved by demolition proceedings to the statutory appellate remedies. It may entertain a suit challenging a demolition order only if it is prima facie of the opinion that the order is a nullity because of jurisdictional error or is outside the statute; it may also examine whether vital procedural requirements were not followed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure preserves civil jurisdiction except where it is expressly or impliedly barred. Sections 343(4)–(5) and 347E of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act bar suits concerning specified demolition proceedings, but the bar does not prevent examination of jurisdictional questions where the statute regulates a pre-existing common-law right. The Court relied on the principles in Secretary of State v. Mask & Co., Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Katikara Chintamani Dora v. Guatreddi Annamanaidu, Desika Charyulu v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Pyx Granite Co. Ltd. v. Ministry of Housing and Local Government, and Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_demolition_action and (action_outside_statutory_scope or jurisdictional_error_established or vital_procedure_not_followed)

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_demolition_action: A person brought a civil suit challenging an action or order concerning demolition of a building.
predicates.action_outside_statutory_scope: The challenged action or order concerned a building or matter to which the statutory scheme did not apply.
predicates.jurisdictional_error_established: The authority's challenged action or order was affected by an error in the exercise of its jurisdiction.
predicates.vital_procedure_not_followed: The authority did not follow a procedural requirement fundamental to the action it took.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges demolition action and the action is outside the statutory scheme, affected by jurisdictional error, or taken without vital procedure, the court may entertain the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary injunction is discretionary and requires a strong prima facie case, favourable balance of convenience, and likely irreparable injury if relief is refused.
material_facts: The suits challenged demolition orders and sought interim relief to prevent demolition while the suits were pending.
The Court noted that interim orders could continue for long periods, perpetuate unlawful construction, and cause injury to defendants and the public.
The Court recognized that interim protection may be needed where a person faces deprivation of property without legal authority or without fundamental procedure being followed.
issues.conclusion: A party is not entitled to an injunction as of right. A court may grant temporary relief only after being satisfied that a strong prima facie case, including as to maintainability, exists, that the balance of convenience favours the applicant, and that refusal would cause irreparable injury.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing discretionary temporary injunctions: the relief preserves the status quo, but requires a strong prima facie case, a favourable balance of convenience, and irreparable injury. Proceedings should not be used to protect or perpetuate a wrong.

rule.if: temporary_injunction_application and strong_prima_facie_case_including_maintainability and balance_of_convenience_favours_applicant and refusal_would_cause_irreparable_injury

predicates.temporary_injunction_application: A party applied for an interim order restraining another party from taking action while a suit was pending.
predicates.strong_prima_facie_case_including_mainta: The applicant presented a strong preliminary case on the merits and on whether the suit could be maintained.
predicates.balance_of_convenience_favours_applicant: The consequences of granting interim relief weigh more heavily in the applicant's favour than the consequences of refusing it.
predicates.refusal_would_cause_irreparable_injury: Refusing interim relief would likely cause the applicant injury that could not be adequately remedied later.

issues.definition: A court may grant a temporary injunction when the applicant has a strong preliminary case, the balance of convenience favours the applicant, and refusing relief would cause irreparable injury.

issues.legal_issue: An injunction without notice requires recorded reasons showing why delay would defeat its purpose and must be limited and accompanied by prompt service and safeguards against further construction.
material_facts: The Court addressed applications seeking injunctions against demolition without first hearing the authority affected by the order.
The procedural rule required notice before an injunction unless delay would defeat the object of granting it, and its proviso required reasons to be recorded for proceeding without notice.

The Court directed that, in the circumstances addressed, an ex parte order last only for a limited period, that the application and supporting documents be served and proof of service filed, and that an extension be granted only after hearing the authority if it had appeared.
The Court also directed the applicant to undertake not to carry out further construction until the injunction application was decided.
issues.conclusion: Before granting an injunction without notice, the court must record reasons for finding that delay would defeat its purpose and consider the relevant factors. The order must be limited in duration, followed by prompt service and proof of service, and may be extended after appearance only after hearing the affected authority; the applicant must undertake not to make further construction pending determination of the application.
issues.legal_principle: Order 39, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires notice before an injunction unless delay would defeat its purpose; the proviso makes recording reasons mandatory when an injunction is granted without notice. The Court applied the principle that a statutory requirement must be followed in the prescribed manner, relying on Taylor v. Taylor, Nazir Ahmed v. Emperor, and Ramachandra Keshav Adke v. Govind Joti Chavare.

predicates.injunction_application_against_demolitio: A party applied for an injunction in a suit concerning action to demolish a building.
predicates.ex_parte_relief_proposed: The court proposed to grant the injunction before hearing the party who would be restrained.
predicates.delay_would_defeat_injunction: The court considered that waiting to give notice would defeat the object of granting the injunction.

issues.definition: When a court proposes an injunction without notice in a demolition-related suit because delay would defeat its purpose, the order requires recorded reasons, limited duration, prompt service and proof of service, a hearing before extension after appearance, and an undertaking against further construction.
